system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2182-06-13 20:48:00 to 2182-06-21 14:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents, was admitted with fever but no abdominal pain or chills. Initial concern for stent obstruction or cholangitis was ruled out by CT imaging, which showed open stents and no biliary dilation. Blood cultures identified ESBL-producing E. coli bacteremia, prompting treatment with meropenem and later transition to outpatient ertapenem via PICC line. The PICC was initially malpositioned but successfully repositioned. His infection resolved, liver function remained stable, and he was discharged home on a two-week course of IV antibiotics with plans to follow up with oncology and undergo scheduled stent exchange. Chemotherapy was to resume after antibiotic completion.
problems: Malignant neoplasm of intrahepatic bile ducts
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Infection with microorganisms resistant to cephalosporins and other B-lactam antibiotics

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure caring for you at ___ 
___.  You were admitted to the hospital for fever.  
We were concerned that you may have infection or blockage of 
your bile ducts.  Therefore, you were evaluated by the ___ team 
who retrieved a plastic stent in one of your bile ducts and 
cleaned your metal stents.  They found that one of your biliary 
ducts was obstructed.  You subsequently underwent percutaneous 
biliary drain placement with the Interventional Radiology 
service.  You did well with the procedure.  Because of the 
drain, it is normal for you to have some abdominal pain at the 
drain site for several weeks.  Because of your abdominal 
discomfort, we started you on pain medication which you may 
continue when you return home.  We also continued you on 
antibiotics; we found that the bacteria growing in your blood 
stream was actually resistant to the antibiotics you were on at 
home.  Therefore, you will be discharged on an antibiotic called 
meropenem.

Please follow-up with your outpatient providers as instructed 
below.

Thank you for allowing us to participate in your care.  All best 
wishes for your recovery.

Sincerely,
Your ___ medical team

are grossly clear.  Cardiomediastinal silhouette is unchanged.

IMPRESSION:  No definite acute cardiopulmonary process.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with unresectable cholangiocarcinoma, s/p stent
placement for recent cholangitis, presenting with E. coli bacteremia and
fevers, needs PTC biliary drain per ERCP. // PTC biliary drain placement given
1 occluded duct during ERCP (___)

COMPARISON:  CT scan ___.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow), Dr.
___ resident) and Dr. ___ radiology attending)
performed the procedure. The attending, Dr. ___ was present and supervising
throughout the procedure.
ANESTHESIA: General anesthesia was administered by the anesthesiology
department.
MEDICATIONS: 3 g unasyn
CONTRAST: 70 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 43 min, 6706 cGyxcm2

PROCEDURE:  1.  Transabdominal ultrasound.
2. Ultrasound guided right percutaneous transhepatic bile duct access.
3. Right cholangiogram
4. ___ right biliary drain.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the
procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the patient and the
patient's wife. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and
placed supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per
___ protocol. The right abdomen was prepped and draped in the usual sterile
fashion.

Under Ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance, a 21G Cook needle was advanced
into right anteriorbiliary system. Several passes were required. Images of the
access were stored on PACS. Once the right anterior biliary system was
opacified, a Headliner wire was advanced under fluoroscopic guidance. The
headliner wire buckled distally. A skin ___ was made over the needle and the
needle was removed over the wire. An Accustick set was advanced over the wire
and the inner stiffener was withdrawn. In order to direct the wire centrally,
a Nitinol wire was passed through the Accustick sheath alongside the
headliner. Then the Accustick set was withdrawn and placed back over the
headliner wire as a safety wire. Using the Nitinol wire as a working wire, the
metal inner stiffener of the Accustick set was placed through a shortened and
a modified omni flush catheter, which was used to advanced the catheter into
the bile duct. Once in the bile duct, the metal inner stiffener and the
Nitinol wire removed and replaced with ___ wire.

A 5 ___ by 20 cm sheath was advanced over the ___ wire and into the bile
duct. The 5 ___ modified omni flush catheter was then reinserted through
the 5 ___ sheath and manipulated down toward the common bile duct. The Omni
flush catheter was exchanged for a 5 ___ Kumpe catheter and the ___ wire
was exchanged for a Glidewire. The glidewire easily passed through the common
bile duct with the assistance of the 5 ___ Kumpe catheter.

The glidewire was exchanged for an Amplatz wire. The 5 ___ Kumpe catheter
was removed and replaced with a 4 mm x 4 cm balloon which was used to dilate
the stricture and the wires of the indwelling Wallstent. This was dine to
fascilitate passage of the PTBD. Following this, the balloon and a 5 ___
sheath were removed and an 8 ___ internal external biliary drain was placed
with approximately 2 cm the sideholes added proximal to the marker. The wire
and inner stiffener were removed and the pigtail was formed. Contrast
injection confirmed appropriate position. The catheter was flushed with
saline, secured with stay sutures to the skin and sterile dressings were
applied. The catheter was attached to a bag.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

Dilated right anterior biliary system with pus. Internal-external 8 ___
biliary drain likely passing through the proximal interstices of the left bare
metal stent.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right anterior ___ internal-external biliary drain.

RECOMMENDATION:  Leave drain open to a bag for several days until fever
results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in today because of a fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had a low-grade fever this morning—about 100.8. But no pain or chills. I’ve been in and out of the hospital so much lately, I’m starting to feel like a regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. That’s tough. But we want to make sure we don’t miss anything serious. You’re on ertapenem at home for that E. coli infection last time, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’m on day 14 of my gemcitabine and cisplatin cycle too. I just finished chemo a couple days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Given your history with cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents, even a small fever can be a sign of infection in the bile ducts—what we call cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I don’t have any belly pain. Shouldn’t I feel that if something’s wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not always. With stents and chronic issues, symptoms can be subtle. We’ve ordered blood work and a chest X-ray just to check things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also have this cough and sinus stuff—it’s been going on for weeks. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but your chest X-ray was clear, so we don’t think it’s pneumonia. We’ll keep an eye on it, but right now, we’re more concerned about your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your white count is normal, but your alkaline phosphatase is elevated, which can suggest a bile duct issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just the fever then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We’re concerned there might be a blockage or infection in the ducts. We’re going to do an ERCP—endoscopy to look inside the ducts and clean or adjust the stents if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? I just had one a few weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a lot. But this one’s important. If there’s a blockage, clearing it can prevent a serious infection. We’ll do it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And will I be asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be under sedation. You’ll feel nothing. We’ll update you afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Johnson. You did well during the ERCP. We found one of your bile ducts was blocked. We cleaned the stents and removed a plastic one that was clogged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s what caused the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. But because the duct was still obstructed, the team decided you need a temporary drain placed directly through the liver into the bile duct. That’s called a PTC drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? How soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow. It’s done by interventional radiology, under imaging guidance. It’ll help drain the bile and reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under general anesthesia, so you’ll be asleep. Afterward, you might have some soreness at the site, but we’ll manage your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The PTC drain was placed successfully. It’s draining bile, and we saw pus, which confirms there was an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pus? So it was infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And we’ve got more news from the lab. The E. coli from your last admission—the one you were treated for with ertapenem—is actually resistant to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, so the antibiotic I’ve been taking isn’t working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s likely why you got sick again. Infectious disease recommends switching to meropenem, which the bacteria are sensitive to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on IV antibiotics again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for 10 days total. You’ll go home with the IV line and a nurse will help you. We’ll also keep you on oral vancomycin to prevent C. diff, since your gut flora might be off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: This is a lot. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you until you’re stable, maybe 4–5 more days. We need to make sure the fever doesn’t come back and the drain is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your latest labs show your white count is coming down—3.7, which is low but improving. That’s a good sign the infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is 3.7 too low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is on the low side, likely from the chemo. But it’s stable. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I restart chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not until after your antibiotics are done. Your oncologist will decide the next steps after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures from yesterday came back negative—no bacteria growing. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s responding well. We’ll keep you on meropenem to finish the full course. The drain is helping a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I notice some drainage into the bag. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It should be dark and bile-colored. That means it’s working. Just keep the site clean and let us know if it becomes red or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Your liver enzymes are improving—alkaline phosphatase is still high but trending down. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the drain—will I have to keep it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. It’s temporary. You’ll follow up with interventional radiology in three months to check if it can be removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I get fever or pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us right away. It could mean the drain is blocked or there’s another infection. You might need another procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your vitals are stable, no fever in 48 hours, and labs are better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with a nurse visiting daily to give meropenem through your PICC line. You’ll finish the 10-day course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take that by mouth until the meropenem is done. Then stop it. It’s just to protect your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds—can I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—pantoprazole for reflux, atenolol for migraines, terazosin for your prostate. Keep taking those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the drain—what do I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Empty the bag twice a day, record the amount, and keep the site clean and dry. A nurse will teach you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might have mild discomfort for a few weeks. Take acetaminophen if needed—avoid ibuprofen because of your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge orders are in. You’re set to go home in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It’s been a long week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It has. But you’re on the mend. Remember: follow up with your oncologist and interventional radiology in three months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or go to the ER if you have fever, severe pain, or the drain stops draining. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma on chemotherapy, was readmitted with fever and found to have recurrent E. coli bacteremia. Initial evaluation revealed no abdominal pain, but elevated liver enzymes prompted an ERCP, which identified a blocked bile duct. A plastic stent was removed and metal stents cleaned. Due to persistent obstruction, a percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain (PTC drain) was placed, with pus noted, confirming cholangitis. Microbiology revealed the E. coli strain was resistant to ertapenem, necessitating a switch to IV meropenem for a 10-day course. He remained afebrile, with improving labs, and was discharged home with IV antibiotics via PICC line, oral vancomycin for C. diff prophylaxis, and instructions for drain care. Follow-up was arranged with oncology and interventional radiology.
